bull.b: Recurring revenue is expanding faster than total sales, improving Rekor’s mix toward contracted and repeatable business. This supports greater revenue visibility, can strengthen customer retention economics, and provides a more durable foundation for margin expansion as the platform scales.

Higher gross margins combined with substantial operating expense reductions are improving the company’s path toward profitability. If these gains persist, Rekor can convert recurring revenue growth into stronger operating leverage and reduce the amount of external funding needed to support its business.

Materially lower leverage gives Rekor more balance-sheet flexibility than in prior years and reduces the burden of debt relative to its equity base. Positive equity provides some support while management works to improve earnings, preserve capital, and fund the transition toward profitability.

bear.b: Rekor remains structurally unprofitable and consumes cash despite improving margins and narrowing losses. Continued negative operating and free cash flow can erode the capital base over time, limit internally funded investment, and leave execution dependent on further cost reductions or outside financing.

Regulatory scrutiny around ALPR can slow customer decisions and complicate adoption across government and commercial markets. Longer sales cycles may delay bookings and revenue conversion, making growth less predictable and increasing the execution burden even when the underlying product pipeline remains active.

Uncertain refinancing creates a meaningful funding risk while Rekor still reports negative cash flow and has not reached sustained adjusted-EBITDA profitability. If refinancing is delayed or less favorable than expected, financial flexibility could narrow and management may need to rely more heavily on cost controls or other funding options.
